title: DepEd Science MATATAG Curriculum — Grade 6 Life Science

customLessons.title: Human Body Systems (Circulatory and Nervous Systems)
objectives: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Circulatory System (heart chambers, valves, arteries, veins, capillaries, blood cells).
Describe the Central Nervous System (brain, spinal cord) and Peripheral Nervous System (sensory and motor neurons).
Explain the reflex arc and how the nervous system regulates all body systems.
customLessons.content:
Advanced coordination in humans is maintained by two master regulatory systems:
- Circulatory System: The four-chambered muscular heart (atria and ventricles) pumps oxygenated blood through arteries to tissues and returns deoxygenated blood through veins. Capillaries facilitate gas and nutrient exchange. Red blood cells carry oxygen via hemoglobin; white blood cells fight pathogens; platelets form clotting scabs.
- Nervous System: Transmits electrical and chemical signals throughout the body:
  - Central Nervous System (CNS): Brain (cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem) processes information; spinal cord acts as the communications highway.
  - Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Sensory and motor neurons transmit impulses.
  - Reflex Arc: An involuntary, split-second protective reaction (e.g., jerking your hand away from a hot pan) that bypasses the brain directly through the spinal cord.

slides.title: Circulatory & Nervous Systems
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Life Science

The body's transport network and electrical control grid: Heart, blood, brain, and nerves.

slides.title: The 4-Chambered Cardiovascular Pump
slides.content:
Double Circulation Loop:
• Right Atrium & Ventricle: Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (Pulmonary Circuit)
• Left Atrium & Ventricle: Powerful muscular pump sending oxygen-rich blood to the entire body (Systemic Circuit)
• Blood Vessels: Arteries (Away from heart), Veins (toward heart with valves), Capillaries (microscopic gas exchange)

slides.title: The Central Nervous System Command
slides.content:
Brain Anatomy & Specializations:
• Cerebrum: Conscious thought, memory, sensory interpretation, reasoning
• Cerebellum: Muscle coordination, posture, balance, precision movement
• Brainstem (Medulla): Involuntary vital reflexes (heartbeat, breathing, swallowing)
• Spinal Cord: The high-speed neural information trunk line
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Sensory receptors detect stimulus (Heat)
Step 2: Sensory neuron transmits impulse to spinal cord
Step 3: Interneuron triggers immediate motor neuron
Step 4: Muscle jerks hand away before brain registers pain!

slides.title: Components of Living Blood
slides.content:
Liquid tissue carrying life:
• Red Blood Cells (RBCs): Packed with iron hemoglobin to transport O2
• White Blood Cells (WBCs): Immune soldiers engulfing bacteria and viruses
• Platelets: Cell fragments forming fibrin clots to seal wounds
• Plasma: 90% water fluid carrying dissolved glucose, hormones, and waste

slides.title: Nervous System Reflex Quiz
slides.content:
Why does your hand pull back from a burning hot stove burner before your brain even realizes you were burned?
A) Your hand has its own brain
B) The reflex arc routes the emergency motor response directly through the spinal cord for speed
C) The muscles contract on their own
D) Blood stops flowing

Correct Answer: B (Spinal reflex arcs bypass the brain for split-second survival!)

customLessons.title: Reproduction in Plants
objectives: Identify floral reproductive organs: stamen (anther, filament) and pistil/carpel (stigma, style, ovary, ovule).
Explain pollination, pollen tube germination, double fertilization, and seed/fruit development.
Analyze seed dispersal mechanisms: wind, water, animal ingestion, and mechanical expulsion.
customLessons.content:
Flowers are the reproductive organs of angiosperms (flowering plants):
- Male organ (Stamen): Anther produces pollen grains containing male sperm nuclei, supported by the filament.
- Female organ (Carpel/Pistil): Stigma receives pollen; style connects to the ovary; ovary contains ovules with egg cells.

Pollination occurs when pollen transfers from anther to stigma via wind or pollinators (bees, bats, butterflies).

Fertilization: A pollen tube grows down the style into the ovule; the sperm fuses with the egg nucleus to form an embryo seed, while the ovary wall swells and matures into a fleshy fruit.

Seed dispersal ensures seeds land far from the parent plant to prevent competition for light and nutrients.

slides.title: Reproduction in Plants
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Life Science

Botanical reproduction: Flower anatomy, pollination pathways, fertilization, and seed dispersal.

slides.title: Flower Anatomy: Stamen & Pistil
slides.content:
The Reproductive Organs:
• Male Organ (Stamen):
  - Anther: Produces golden pollen grains carrying male sperm cells
  - Filament: Slender stalk holding the anther aloft
• Female Organ (Pistil / Carpel):
  - Stigma: Sticky surface catching airborne or insect-carried pollen
  - Style: Neck tube through which pollen tubes grow
  - Ovary: Swollen base containing ovules (prospective seeds)

slides.title: From Pollen Grain to Fruit
slides.content:
The Steps of Plant Fertilization:
1. Pollination: Pollen lands on sticky stigma
2. Tube Growth: Pollen grain germinates a tube down the style
3. Fertilization: Sperm fuses with ovule egg cell
4. Transformation: The fertilized ovule becomes a hard SEED; the surrounding ovary wall expands into the FRUIT!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Pollen lands on stigma
Step 2: Tube grows down style
Step 3: Sperm fertilizes ovule egg
Step 4: Ovule becomes seed, Ovary becomes fruit

slides.title: Seed Dispersal Engineering
slides.content:
Escaping the parent tree's shade:
• Wind: Dandelion parachutes and winged Narra tree seeds
• Water: Buoyant fibrous coconut husks drifting across oceans
• Animals: Sweet mango fruits eaten and seeds dropped; prickly burrs clinging to fur
• Explosive: Touch-me-not seedpods bursting open under tension

slides.title: Plant Reproduction Quiz
slides.content:
Following successful plant fertilization, what does the flower's ovary develop into?
A) A green leaf
B) A fleshy fruit protecting the seeds
C) A taproot
D) A new flower petal

Correct Answer: B (The ovary wall swells and ripens into fruit!)

customLessons.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
objectives: Classify animals into Vertebrates (with backbones) and Invertebrates (without backbones).
Distinguish characteristics of the 5 vertebrate classes: Fish, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds, and Mammals.
Classify major invertebrate phyla: Arthropods, Mollusks, Annelids, Cnidarians, and Echinoderms.
customLessons.content:
The Animal Kingdom is divided into two major divisions based on the presence of an internal vertebral column:
- Vertebrates (Chordates): Possess an endoskeleton and spinal column:
  1. Fish: Ectothermic, aquatic, gills, scales, fins.
  2. Amphibians: Ectothermic, smooth moist skin, dual water-land life cycle.
  3. Reptiles: Ectothermic, dry scaly skin, amniotic shelled eggs, breathe with lungs.
  4. Birds: Endothermic, feathers, hollow bones, beaks, lay hard-shelled eggs.
  5. Mammals: Endothermic, hair/fur, mammary glands for milk, give live birth.
- Invertebrates: Make up over 95% of animal species!
  - Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids) with chitinous exoskeletons and jointed legs.
  - Mollusks (snails, clams, squids) with soft bodies often protected by calcium shells.
  - Annelids (earthworms, leeches) with segmented bodies.
  - Cnidarians (corals, jellyfish) with stinging nematocysts.
  - Echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) with spiny skins and radial symmetry.

slides.title: Vertebrates & Invertebrates
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Life Science

Classifying the Animal Kingdom: Backbone possessors versus the vast invertebrate empire.

slides.title: The Five Vertebrate Classes
slides.content:
Animals with Internal Spinal Columns:
• Fish: Scales, fins, gills, cold-blooded (Tilapia, bangus)
• Amphibians: Moist skin, metamorphosis, aquatic eggs (Frogs, toads)
• Reptiles: Dry scaly skin, lungs, leathery shelled eggs (Lizards, crocodiles, snakes)
• Birds: Feathers, hollow flight bones, warm-blooded (Philippine eagle, maya)
• Mammals: Hair/fur, mammary glands, warm-blooded (Whales, bats, carabao, humans)

slides.title: Ectotherms vs Endotherms
slides.content:
Body Temperature Regulation:
• Ectothermic (Cold-Blooded): Body temperature depends on external sun/water (Fish, amphibians, reptiles)
• Endothermic (Warm-Blooded): Generate internal metabolic body heat, maintaining steady temperature (Birds and mammals)
slides.mediaUrl:
Has a backbone? -> Vertebrate
Has hair and nurses young? -> Mammal
Has feathers and beak? -> Bird
Cold-blooded with dry scales? -> Reptile

slides.title: The Invertebrate Majority (>95% of Species)
slides.content:
Creatures without backbones:
• Arthropods: Jointed legs & chitinous exoskeleton (Crabs, spiders, bees, butterflies)
• Mollusks: Soft unsegmented bodies, often with shells (Snails, giant clams, squids)
• Annelids: Segmented cylindrical bodies (Earthworms, leeches)
• Cnidarians: Stinging tentacles around central mouth (Jellyfish, sea anemones, corals)
• Echinoderms: Spiny skin and 5-part radial symmetry (Starfish, sea urchins)

slides.title: Vertebrate Classification Quiz
slides.content:
Why is a dolphin classified as a mammal rather than a fish, even though it swims in the sea?
A) It lays eggs in coral reefs
B) It has hair, breathes atmospheric air with lungs, and nurses young with milk
C) It has scales and gills
D) It is cold-blooded

Correct Answer: B (Dolphins are warm-blooded placental marine mammals!)

customLessons.title: Ecosystem Relationships (Food Webs, Interaction Among Living Things, Biotic and Abiotic Factors in an Ecosystem)
objectives: Construct and analyze complex food webs and determine the consequences of ecological disruptions.
Differentiate symbiotic ecological relationships: Mutualism, Commensalism, Parasitism, Predation, and Competition.
Explain the cycling of matter and energy between biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components.
customLessons.content:
An ecosystem is a biological community of interacting organisms (biotic factors) and their physical environment (abiotic factors: temperature, sunlight, soil, water, atmospheric gases).

Food Webs: Natural feeding relationships are not single chains but interconnected webs. Removing a keystone predator (like sharks or Philippine eagles) triggers trophic cascades that destabilize the entire ecosystem.

Ecological Symbiosis:
- Mutualism: Both species benefit (+ / +), e.g., coral polyps and zooxanthellae algae, bees and flowers.
- Commensalism: One benefits, the other is unharmed (+ / 0), e.g., orchids growing on tree trunks, barnacles on whales.
- Parasitism: One benefits at the host's expense (+ / -), e.g., mosquitoes, intestinal worms, tick on dog.
- Predation: Predator hunts and consumes prey (+ / -).
- Competition: Organisms compete for limited resources (food, space, mates).

slides.title: Ecosystem Relationships & Food Webs
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 2 Life Science

Complex ecological webs: Food webs, symbiotic partnerships, and biotic-abiotic cycles.

slides.title: Biotic vs Abiotic Factors
slides.content:
The Two Halves of Every Ecosystem:
• Biotic Factors (Living): Plants, herbivores, carnivores, fungi, bacteria
• Abiotic Factors (Non-Living Physical): Sunlight intensity, temperature, rainfall, dissolved oxygen, soil minerals, pH
• Constant interaction: Sunlight and water dictate what vegetation thrives; vegetation feeds the animal community

slides.title: Food Webs: Interconnected Stability
slides.content:
Why webs are stronger than single chains:
• Animals eat diverse prey species, not just one food source
• Keystone Predators: Keep prey populations from exploding and overconsuming vegetation
• Trophic Cascade: Eliminating top predators triggers ecological collapse!
slides.mediaUrl:
Producers: Seagrass & Phytoplankton
Primary: Zooplankton & Herbivore Fish
Secondary: Squid, Snapper, Reef Crabs
Tertiary / Apex: Reef Sharks & Sea Turtles

slides.title: The Five Symbiotic Relationships
slides.content:
Living together in close association:
• Mutualism (+ / +): Both benefit (Corals & algae; Bees & flowers)
• Commensalism (+ / 0): One benefits, other unaffected (Bird nest in tree; Orchids on bark)
• Parasitism (+ / -): Parasite feeds on host (Ticks on dog; Tapeworms in intestine)
• Predation (+ / -): Predator kills prey
• Competition (- / -): Fighting for limited resources

slides.title: Ecosystem Symbiosis Quiz
slides.content:
What ecological relationship exists between an aerial orchid growing on the trunk of a giant narra tree?
A) Parasitism (orchid steals tree sap)
B) Commensalism (orchid gains sunlight height; tree is neither helped nor harmed)
C) Predation
D) Mutualism

Correct Answer: B (Commensalism: orchid benefits while tree is unharmed!)
